jsnvu6-e180189-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 5: whether, besides acquired intellectual habits, we need theological habits, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e119.summary: Turns from habits in general to faith, which is a theological habit, and asks whether we need theological habits besides acquired moral and intellectual ones. Objection: such habits would be needed only for supernatural beatitude, but baptized infants who die attain it without seeming to need them.
claims: Theological habits would be needed only for supernatural beatitude (objection)
Baptized infants reach beatitude without them (objection)

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e145.summary: Second objection: perfections are proportioned to what they perfect; our only perfectible powers are the rational by essence, perfected by intellectual virtue, and the rational by participation, perfected by moral virtue; so there is no room for a third genus of habit.
claims: Only two kinds of perfectible powers exist, so only two genera of habit (objection)
concepts: rational by essence vs. by participation

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e164.summary: Argument for the opposite: the theological habits are faith, hope, and charity, all of which Scripture shows we need (Heb. 11; Titus 3; 1 Cor. 13).
claims: Faith, hope, and charity are necessary according to Scripture

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e182.summary: Outline of the response: whether we need habits beyond those acquirable from pure naturals; how many and which they are; and how they are distinguished from other habits.

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e198.summary: First article: we need theological habits beyond naturally acquired ones. Acts ordering us to supernatural beatitude must be no less perfect than those ordering us to natural beatitude, which proceed from powers perfected by habits; and since supernatural beatitude is of another kind, the habits disposing to it must be too. They are called theological because they have God for object, order their acts to God as beatifying end, and are taught by divine word alone. But the orderings differ: some natural acts attain or even constitute natural beatitude (Ethics X), whereas theological acts in this life order us to supernatural beatitude only by way of merit, as way to term, and none is beatitude itself.
claims: We need theological habits beyond naturally acquired habits
Theological habits are specifically distinct because supernatural beatitude is of another kind
They are called theological because God is their object and end and they are known only by revelation
Theological acts in via order to beatitude only meritoriously, not constitutively

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e268.summary: Second article: there are exactly three theological habits. Acts ordered to supernatural beatitude relate to it as merit to reward, and there is no merit without charity. One cannot order acts to an end without knowing it, and supernatural beatitude is not knowable by natural reason, so it must be believed on God's revelation, which is faith. One does not tend to an end unless it is possible to attain, and the supernatural end can be had only by another's gift, so hope relies on divine liberality as faith relies on divine truth. These three are required and also sufficient.
claims: Charity is required because there is no merit without it
Faith is required because supernatural beatitude is known only by revelation
Hope is required because the end is attainable only by divine gift
Exactly three theological virtues are necessary and sufficient

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e327.summary: Third article: theological habits differ formally from natural moral and intellectual habits because their objects differ formally. Other habits have created objects or, like metaphysical wisdom, consider God under a naturally knowable aspect; theological habits have God as exceeding intellect and will—faith under truth elevated beyond natural intellect, hope under goodness exceeding human capacity, charity under goodness that communicates itself.
claims: Theological habits are distinguished by formally distinct objects
Natural wisdom considers God under a naturally knowable aspect
Faith, hope, and charity have God as object under truth, arduous goodness, and self-communicating goodness respectively

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e366.summary: Reply to the first objection: either baptized infants have infused theological habits, or, if not, they differ from adults, reaching beatitude solely by Christ's merit communicated through baptism, while adults need their own merit (James 2: faith without works is dead), for which theological habits are required. The first answer is judged truer.
claims: Baptized infants more probably have infused theological habits
Adults need their own merit, which requires theological habits

jsnvu6-e180189-d1e391.summary: Reply to the second objection: habits are distinguished not only by subject but also by object; the theological habits' objects differ formally from those of moral and intellectual habits, so they are distinct even though sharing the same subject.
claims: Habits are distinguished by object as well as by subject

jsnvu6-e180189.summary: Question 5 moves from habits in general to faith by asking whether, besides naturally acquired moral and intellectual habits, we need theological habits. Objections: infants reach beatitude without them, and we have only two kinds of perfectible rational power. Durandus answers that acts ordering us to supernatural beatitude must proceed from powers perfected by habits of a different kind than those ordering us to natural beatitude. These habits are theological because God is their object and end and they are known only from revelation. Unlike natural acts, which can constitute natural felicity, they order us to beatitude in this life only by merit. There are exactly three: charity, without which there is no merit; faith, because the end is known only by revelation; and hope, because the end is attainable only by divine gift. They differ formally from natural habits by their objects: God as truth beyond the intellect, as goodness beyond human power, and as self-communicating goodness. Baptized infants probably have infused habits, and habits are distinguished by object as well as subject.
claims: Theological habits are necessary in addition to naturally acquired habits
Exactly three theological virtues—faith, hope, charity—are necessary and sufficient
Theological habits are distinguished by formally distinct objects
Theological acts in via order to beatitude only meritoriously
